extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, playwrights, literary critics, and educated readers interested in composition and theatrical criticism
extracted.subtask_short: writing sublime poetry and tragic drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for composing elevated (sublime) poetry and for dramatic writing/production—especially how to achieve loftiness of sentiment, maintain tonal consistency in tragedy, and use classical/allusive models. Also includes pedagogical methods for forming moral judgment in young writers/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of dialogue in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Should your People in Tragedy always talk to be understood? Why, there is not a single Sentence in this Play that I do not know the Meaning of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The remark argues for dialogue that can be readily understood by the audience rather than obscurity for its own sake; treat lines so the meaning is accessible even in elevated drama. (Presented as Sir Roger's practical, 'natural Criticism' while watching the play.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tacking comic epilogues onto tragedies (tonal consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most unnatural Tack of the Comick Tail to the Tragick Head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not undermine the emotional effect built through a tragedy by appending a merry epilogue; doing so jumbles the audience's feelings, dissipates the tragic impression, and can make noble achievements seem 'silly and romantick.' Consider preserving the unity of tone so the audience's emotional response remains 'uniform, and all of a Piece.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience refreshment but weigh consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The common defence is that 'the Minds of the Audience must be refreshed, and Gentlemen and Ladies not sent away... with too dismal and melancholy Thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some argue for comic relief to prevent melancholy, the page advises caution—refreshment should not erode the intended moral or emotional effect. Weigh whether a lighter closing is appropriate given the play's purpose and the potential cultural spillover (e.g., into church music).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit music and ancillary performance to place and business
rubrics_metrics.description: Those fingering Gentlemen should be informed, that they ought to suit their Airs to the Place and Business; and that the Musician is obliged to keep to the Text as much as the Preacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music and musical interpolations should match the genre, subject, and setting (e.g., avoid jocular organ voluntaries after solemn sermons or tragic plays). Maintain appropriateness between form and context to avoid dissipating intended dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced characterization: praise virtues but expose faults
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be great Care taken how the Example of any particular Person is recommended to them in gross; instead of which, they ought to be taught wherein such a Man, though great in some respects, was weak and faulty in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting exemplary figures (in instruction or in narrative), avoid uncritical hero-worship; point out both strengths and weaknesses so readers/students learn to judge character complexity rather than idolize. Use concrete examples from biography/literature to illustrate mixed character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach moral judgment through analytical writing exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: It would not be more proper that a Boy should be tasked once or twice a Week to write down his Opinion of such Persons and Things as occur to him in his Reading; that he should descant upon the actions... censure or approve any particular Action...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use written exercises that require students (or writers-in-training) to evaluate actions and motives, justify their judgments, compare characters (e.g., Turnus vs. Aeneas), and identify moral elements in speeches—this strengthens judgment and instills a sense of virtue in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form virtue by practice, example, and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Xenophon's Schools of Equity ... governors spent most part of the Day in hearing their mutual Accusations one against the other... taught them how to give Judgment against those who were found to be any ways guilty...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and civic virtues are best inculcated through regular practice, peer accountability, and applied exercises (e.g., reporting daily use of time or judging peers' conduct). In pedagogical writing or didactic literature, embed practical activities that cultivate habits rather than merely conveying precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: First impressions shape the mind strongly
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Youth cannot be too soon taught the Principles of Virtue, seeing the first Impressions which are made on the Mind are always the strongest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers and educators: shape early exposures deliberately; openings, early character portrayals, and first lessons have disproportionate formative power—use them to establish moral or thematic direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate celebrated predecessors to catch the spirit (without slavish copying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the Rules ... he should imitate the most celebrated Authors who have gone before him... By this means one great Genius often catches the Flame from another, and writes in his Spirit, without copying servilely after him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study masterworks (Homer, Virgil, Scripture, Longinus) and appropriate their spirit, modes, and strengths for your subject matter—but avoid mere servile imitation. Let the imitation inform tone, grand conceits, and structural choices while remaining original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand relation between pathos and the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a Loftiness in Sentiments, where there is no Passion... The Pathetick ... may animate and inflame the Sublime, but is not essential to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two related but distinct modes: the sublime (composed majesty, magnificent ideas) and the pathetick (strong passion). Great writing can achieve sublimity through serene grandeur rather than overt emotional tumult; decide which mode suits the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate allusions (scriptural, classical) fitted to subject and readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton...has numberless Allusions to [Scripture] through the whole course of this Book... the great Critick ... has taken notice of the sublime Manner in which the Lawgiver of the Jews has describ'd the Creation...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select allusions and precedents that resonate with your subject and audience (e.g., Scripture for Creation themes, Homer for epic diction). Properly qualified allusions elevate tone and provide cultural depth—use them judiciously to match readers' imaginative pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose majestic, measured diction for scenes of grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: The Author appears in a kind of composed and sedate Majesty... they abound with as magnificent Ideas... The Angels encouraging our first Parents in a modest pursuit after Knowledge... are very just and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sublime passages, favor stately, measured language and grand conceptions over turbulent rhetoric; build imagery (e.g., chariots, gates of heaven, silence of troubled waves) that conveys vastness and order. Use controlled elevation rather than chaotic passion to achieve a calm sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When treating a poetical subject, consider how earlier masters would speak
rubrics_metrics.description: If he writes on a poetical Subject, he should consider how Homer would have spoken on such an Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze classical exemplars for tone, diction, and narrative decision-making relevant to your subject; borrow their strategies for majestic description, simile, and epic procedure, adapting them to contemporary aims.
